what_its_for: Quetiapine is used to treat several mental health conditions. These include schizophrenia (a condition that affects how you think and feel), bipolar disorder (extreme mood swings between highs and lows), and major depression (when taken with other antidepressants). It helps balance certain chemicals in your brain to improve your mood, thinking, and behavior.
how_to_take: Take quetiapine exactly as your doctor tells you. You can take it with or without food. If you are taking the extended-release tablet (Seroquel XR), swallow it whole — do not crush, chew, or break it. The regular tablet can be split if needed. Try to take it at the same time each day to keep a steady level in your body. Do not stop taking it suddenly without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better.
dosing: Your dose will depend on the condition being treated and how your body responds. Doses are usually started low and slowly increased by your doctor. Typical doses range from 50 mg to 800 mg per day, taken once or twice daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions — never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — unless it is almost time for your next dose. In that case, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store quetiapine at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not flush unused medication down the toilet — ask your pharmacist about a safe drug take-back program.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking quetiapine, as it can increase drowsiness and dizziness. Do not drive, operate heavy machinery, or do other activities that require alertness until you know how this medication affects you. Avoid overheating and dehydration, especially in hot weather or during exercise, as quetiapine can affect your body's ability to regulate temperature. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice, as it may increase the amount of medicine in your blood. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about all other medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: thoughts of harming yourself or others, sudden high fever with stiff muscles and confusion (signs of a rare but serious reaction called Neuroleptic Malignant Syndrome), uncontrolled movements of your face, tongue, or body, fast or irregular heartbeat, severe dizziness or fainting, signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, urination, or blurred vision, unusual weight gain, or a prolonged or painful erection (in males). Also call your doctor if your mood gets worse or you feel more anxious or agitated, especially in the first few weeks.
when_it_works: You may start to notice some improvement — such as better sleep or feeling calmer — within the first few days to one week. However, it may take 4 to 6 weeks or longer to feel the full benefits of quetiapine. Be patient and keep taking it as prescribed, even if you do not feel better right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first.
special_populations: Older adults: Quetiapine should be used with extra caution in elderly patients, especially those with dementia, as it may increase the risk of stroke or death. Older adults may also be more sensitive to side effects like dizziness and falls. Pregnancy: Talk to your doctor if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Babies born to mothers who took this medicine in the last trimester may have temporary withdrawal symptoms. Children and teenagers: Quetiapine is approved for some conditions in children aged 10 and older, but must be closely monitored by a doctor. Kidney or liver problems: Your doctor may need to adjust your dose if you have kidney or liver disease.
